text: In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace…
reflection: Paul packs the whole gospel into one rich sentence: "In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace." Redemption means being bought back, set free at a price. In the ancient world, the word was used for freeing a slave. We were held captive by sin and guilt, unable to free ourselves. But Jesus paid the price with His own blood. Now we have forgiveness, not a partial forgiveness, but complete. And notice the measure: according to the riches of His grace. God does not forgive us out of a small, reluctant supply. He forgives from an overflowing treasury that will never run dry. Whatever you have done, it is not too big for the riches of His grace. As we begin this month focused on grace, mercy, and redemption, receive His forgiveness fully. Let go of the chains He has already broken, and walk today in the freedom He purchased for you.
question: What chain that Jesus has already broken are you still carrying?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You redeemed me with Your blood and forgave all my sins according to the riches of Your grace. Help me let go of broken chains and walk in Your freedom today. Amen.

text: Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness.
reflection: David wrote this psalm after his darkest failure. He had committed adultery and arranged for a man's death. When confronted, he did not make excuses. He cried out, "Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness." David knew he could not fix what he had done. Only God could deliver him. And notice what he promises in response: singing. A heart set free from guilt cannot stay silent. It overflows with praise. Perhaps there is something in your past that still weighs on you. You may think it is too terrible for God to forgive. David's prayer shows otherwise. The God of salvation can deliver even from the heaviest guilt. Honest confession opens the door to His mercy. Today, bring whatever you have been hiding into His light. Ask for His deliverance. And when you feel the weight lift, let your heart sing of His goodness.
question: What have you been hiding that you could bring honestly into God's light today?
prayer: God of my salvation, I cannot fix what I have done, but You can deliver me. I bring my failures into Your light, and I will sing of Your goodness. Amen.

text: But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they.
reflection: At an important meeting in Jerusalem, the early church debated whether Gentile believers needed to keep the Jewish law to be saved. Peter stood up and made it clear: "But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they." Notice the humility in his words. Peter, a Jewish apostle who had walked with Jesus, did not say that Gentiles would be saved like him. He said that he would be saved just like them. Everyone comes to God the same way, through grace alone. This truth tears down walls between people. No one gets to look down on anyone else. Whatever our background, culture, or history, we all stand on the same ground: undeserved grace received by faith. Today, let that truth shape how you see others. Treat every person as a fellow recipient of grace. And rest in knowing that your salvation depends not on your record, but on the grace of Jesus.
question: How might it change the way you treat others to see each one as a fellow recipient of grace?
prayer: Lord Jesus, I am saved by Your grace, just like everyone else. Keep me humble, and help me treat every person as one who needs and receives Your grace. Amen.

text: But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption…
reflection: Paul reminds the Corinthians where their life truly comes from: "But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption." Everything we need is found in Jesus. Do you lack wisdom for a decision? Christ is your wisdom. Do you feel unworthy before God? Christ is your righteousness. Are you struggling to grow in holiness? Christ is your sanctification. Do you feel trapped by your past? Christ is your redemption. This is the beauty of being in Christ. We do not have to produce these things on our own. We receive them by being united with Him. The Corinthians had been boasting in human wisdom and status, but Paul points them to the only One worth boasting in. Today, instead of looking within for what you lack, look to Jesus. Whatever you need, He has become that for you. Rest in Him, and let your confidence be in His sufficiency, not your own.
question: What do you feel you lack today, and how has Christ become that very thing for you?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You are my wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. Instead of looking within for what I lack, help me look to You and rest in Your sufficiency. Amen.

text: I do not frustrate the grace of God: for if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain.
reflection: Paul makes a bold argument: "I do not frustrate the grace of God: for if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain." If we could earn our way to God by keeping rules, then the cross would have been unnecessary. Jesus would have died for nothing. But He did not die in vain. He died because we could never be righteous on our own. To try to earn what Jesus already paid for is to set aside His grace. Many of us slip into this without realizing it. We feel closer to God on days when we perform well and distant on days when we fail. We keep spiritual scorecards. But grace invites us to stop striving and start receiving. Our good works matter, but they are a grateful response to grace, not a payment for it. Today, refuse to frustrate the grace of God. Let go of the scorecard. Rest in what Christ has done. His death was not in vain; it was enough.
question: Where are you still keeping a scorecard with God instead of resting in what Christ has done?
prayer: Lord, I will not frustrate Your grace. I let go of my scorecard and rest in what Jesus has done. His death was not in vain; it was enough. Amen.

text: Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ: Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied.
reflection: Peter begins his letter by describing the whole Trinity at work in our salvation. We are "Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit, unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ." The Father chose us. The Spirit sets us apart. The Son cleanses us. Every Person of the Godhead is involved in bringing us home. And then comes the blessing: "Grace unto you, and peace, be multiplied." Not just added, but multiplied. Peter was writing to believers scattered and suffering for their faith. They needed more than a little grace. They needed grace upon grace, peace upon peace. God's supply is not limited. When your needs increase, His grace increases to meet them. If you are facing a hard season, ask God to multiply His grace and peace in your life. The God who planned your salvation, carried it out, and applies it to your heart will not leave you lacking.
question: In what hard season do you need God to multiply His grace and peace?
prayer: Father, Son, and Spirit, thank You for choosing, cleansing, and setting me apart. Multiply Your grace and peace in my life, especially in this hard season. Amen.

text: That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord.
reflection: Paul describes two kingdoms in conflict. One is ruled by sin, and it leads to death. The other is ruled by grace, and it leads to life: "That as sin hath reigned unto death, even so might grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life by Jesus Christ our Lord." Sin is a cruel king. It promises freedom but delivers bondage. It ends in death. But grace is a kind and powerful King. It reigns through the righteousness of Jesus, and its rule ends in eternal life. Notice that grace does not merely visit; it reigns. It takes the throne. That means grace is stronger than your failures, stronger than your past, and stronger than the habits that pull you down. Where sin abounded, grace abounds much more. Today, let grace have the throne of your life. When guilt or temptation tries to rule, remember who your King is. You live under the reign of grace, and its kingdom leads to life.
question: When guilt or temptation tries to rule you, how can you remember that grace is your King?
prayer: Lord, let grace reign on the throne of my life. When guilt or temptation tries to rule, remind me that I live under the kind reign of grace that leads to life. Amen.

text: Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began…
reflection: Before you were born, before the mountains were formed, before the world began, God had grace in mind for you. Paul writes that God "hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began." This is staggering. Your salvation was not a last-minute rescue plan. It was not based on how well you would perform. It was rooted in God's eternal purpose and freely given grace. That means your worth before God does not rise and fall with your achievements. You were loved and planned for before you ever did anything good or bad. And you are called to a holy purpose, a life set apart for Him. Today, rest in this ancient grace. When you feel unworthy, remember that grace was given before you could earn it. And walk in your holy calling, not to earn His love, but because you already have it.
question: When you feel unworthy, how does it help to know God's grace was given before you could earn it?
prayer: Lord, You gave me grace in Christ before the world began. When I feel unworthy, remind me of Your ancient grace, and help me walk in my holy calling. Amen.

text: And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation…
reflection: John was given a glimpse of heaven's worship, and he heard a new song rising before the throne: "Thou art worthy … for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation." The Lamb who was slain is worthy of all praise. Why? Because He redeemed people from every corner of the earth. Every language, every culture, every nation is represented in that great choir. This is the beautiful scope of God's saving work. It is not limited to one group or one kind of person. The blood of Jesus is powerful enough to redeem anyone, anywhere. And one day, a multitude from every background will sing together with one voice. Today, let this vision shape how you see people who are different from you. They may be future members of that heavenly choir. Celebrate the diversity of God's family, and join the song of praise to the Lamb who redeemed us.
question: How can you see people who are different from you as future voices in heaven's choir?
prayer: Worthy Lamb, You were slain and redeemed people from every nation and tongue. Teach me to celebrate Your diverse family and to join the song of praise to You. Amen.

text: Thus saith the LORD, Keep ye judgment, and do justice: for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed.
reflection: God speaks to His people with both a call and a promise: "Keep ye judgment, and do justice: for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed." The call is to live rightly, to practice fairness, and to treat others justly. The promise is that God's salvation is near. These two belong together. Because God's saving work is coming, His people are called to live in a way that reflects His character now. When we act with justice and integrity, we become signs of the salvation that is on its way. We give the world a preview of God's kingdom. This is not about earning salvation. It is about living in a way that matches the God who saves. Today, look for one practical way to do justice. Treat someone fairly who is often treated unfairly. Speak up for someone who has no voice. Be honest when it would be easier to cut corners. In doing so, you announce that God's salvation is near.
question: Who is often treated unfairly that you could treat with justice and care today?
prayer: Lord, Your salvation is near. Help me keep judgment and do justice, treating others fairly and speaking up for those who have no voice. Amen.

text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
reflection: This may be one of the most comforting promises in the Bible: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." Notice the two words used to describe God. He is faithful, meaning He keeps His promise to forgive. He is just, meaning forgiveness is right because Jesus has already paid the penalty. God is not grudgingly letting us off the hook. He is acting in perfect faithfulness and justice. And the cleansing is complete: from all unrighteousness, not just some. Confession is simply agreeing with God about what is true. It is bringing into the light what we would rather hide. That can feel frightening, but this verse turns confession into a doorway of freedom. Today, take some time to be honest with God. Name what is weighing on your conscience. Then receive His forgiveness fully. You do not need to keep carrying what He has already washed away.
question: What is weighing on your conscience that you need to confess and let God wash away?
prayer: Lord, You are faithful and just to forgive. I confess what weighs on my conscience, and I receive Your cleansing. Help me stop carrying what You have washed away. Amen.

text: He that followeth after righteousness and mercy findeth life, righteousness, and honour.
reflection: Proverbs gives a promise that is easy to remember and powerful to live: "He that followeth after righteousness and mercy findeth life, righteousness, and honour." Notice the word followeth. It describes pursuit, chasing after something with determination. The one who pursues doing right and showing mercy ends up finding much more than they were seeking. They find life in its fullness. They find righteousness. And they find honor, not the shallow fame of the world, but the lasting respect that comes from a life well lived. Righteousness and mercy belong together. Righteousness without mercy can become harsh. Mercy without righteousness can become careless. But when we pursue both, we reflect the heart of God, who is perfectly just and abundantly merciful. Today, chase after what is right and kind. When you face a choice, ask which path is both good and gracious. You may be surprised how much life you find along the way.
question: When you face a choice today, which path is both right and merciful?
prayer: Lord, give me a heart that chases after righteousness and mercy. When I face a choice, lead me in the path that is both good and gracious. Amen.

text: Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
reflection: Imagine being invited to approach the throne of the King of the universe. Most of us would expect to come trembling, unsure of our welcome. But Hebrews invites us differently: "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need." Notice what kind of throne it is. Not a throne of judgment for those in Christ, but a throne of grace. The One who sits there knows our weaknesses, because Jesus Himself was tempted in every way we are. He understands. So we can come boldly, not because we are worthy, but because He is gracious. And we will find exactly what we need: mercy for our failures and grace for our struggles. Whatever you are facing today, you do not have to face it alone. Come to the throne. Bring your need. Ask boldly. Grace is waiting, and it always arrives right on time.
question: What need can you bring boldly to the throne of grace today?
prayer: Lord, You invite me to come boldly to Your throne of grace. I bring You my need today, and I ask for mercy and grace to help right on time. Amen.

text: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God…
reflection: These words are among the most beloved in all of Scripture: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." Salvation is a gift. It is not a wage we earn, a prize we win, or a reward for being good enough. It is given freely by God's grace. Faith is simply the empty hand that receives it. And Paul is careful to add that even this is not of ourselves. We cannot take credit. Every part of our salvation comes from God's generous heart. This truth brings both humility and relief. Humility, because we have nothing to boast about. Relief, because we do not have to carry the impossible burden of earning God's love. A gift can only be received. Today, receive it again. Thank God for the gift of salvation. And let gratitude, not pressure, be the motivation for how you live. You are saved by grace, through faith, as a gift.
question: Are you living today from gratitude for grace or from pressure to earn it?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the gift of salvation, by grace through faith. Let gratitude, not pressure, shape how I live today. Amen.

text: Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.
reflection: Paul wrote to the church in Philippi from a prison cell, yet his greeting overflowed with warmth: "Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ." Even in chains, Paul wanted his friends to have the two gifts that sustained him. Grace for every need, and peace for every worry. This is remarkable. Paul did not wait for his circumstances to improve before he spoke of grace and peace. He had found them in the middle of hardship. And they came from a sure source: God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace and peace are not dependent on comfortable surroundings. They are rooted in a relationship with God. That means you can experience them today, whatever your situation. Perhaps you feel confined by illness, responsibilities, or circumstances you did not choose. Grace can still reach you there, and peace can still guard your heart. Receive them now as gifts from your Father.
question: What circumstance confines you, and how can grace and peace still reach you there?
prayer: Father, grace and peace come from You, even in hard places. Reach me where I feel confined, and let Your peace guard my heart today. Amen.

text: He shall receive the blessing from the LORD, and righteousness from the God of his salvation.
reflection: Psalm 24 asks who may stand in God's holy place, and the answer describes a person with clean hands and a pure heart. Then comes the promise: "He shall receive the blessing from the LORD, and righteousness from the God of his salvation." Notice the word receive. The righteousness that allows us to stand before God is not something we manufacture. It is received from Him as a gift. Even the clean hands and pure heart are fruits of His saving work in us. God is described here as the God of salvation. That is His nature. He delights to save, to bless, and to make people right with Himself. When we come to Him with sincere hearts, He does not send us away empty. He fills our hands with blessing. Today, come to God honestly. Ask Him to cleanse your hands and purify your heart. Then receive the righteousness and blessing He freely gives. The God of your salvation is generous.
question: What do you need God to cleanse in your hands or heart today?
prayer: God of my salvation, cleanse my hands and purify my heart. I receive the righteousness and blessing You freely give, with gratitude and joy. Amen.

text: But Israel shall be saved in the LORD with an everlasting salvation: ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end.
reflection: Through Isaiah, God made a promise that reaches across the ages: "But Israel shall be saved in the LORD with an everlasting salvation: ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end." Notice the word everlasting. God's salvation is not temporary. It does not expire, wear thin, or depend on how strong we feel. It lasts forever. And because it is everlasting, those who trust in Him will never be put to shame. Shame is one of the heaviest burdens a person can carry. It whispers that we are not enough, that we will be exposed and rejected. But God promises that those saved in Him will not be ashamed or confused, world without end. Your story will not end in disgrace. In the Lord, it ends in glory. Today, if shame has been speaking loudly in your heart, answer it with this promise. Your salvation is everlasting, and in Him you will never be put to shame.
question: What shame has been speaking loudly in your heart, and how does God's everlasting salvation answer it?
prayer: Lord, Your salvation is everlasting, and in You I will never be put to shame. Silence the voice of shame in my heart with the truth of Your promise. Amen.

text: Grace be to you and peace from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.
reflection: Paul wrote 2 Corinthians to a church that had hurt him deeply. There had been conflict, criticism, and painful misunderstanding. Yet he opened his letter the same way he always did: "Grace be to you and peace from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ." Before addressing any problems, Paul extended grace. That is a beautiful lesson for our relationships. When there is tension with someone, our instinct might be to start with complaints or demands. But Paul led with blessing. He wanted the Corinthians to receive God's grace and peace before anything else. The next verses go on to praise the God of all comfort, who comforts us so we can comfort others. Grace received becomes grace extended. Today, think of a relationship that has been strained. Before you say anything else, wish that person grace and peace. Pray for them. Let God's grace soften your words and open the way toward healing.
question: Whom could you wish grace and peace to before addressing a strained relationship?
prayer: Lord, before I speak of hurts or problems, help me extend grace. Bless the person I find difficult with grace and peace, and soften my words toward healing. Amen.

text: But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever. Amen.
reflection: Peter's final words in his final letter are an invitation to keep growing: "But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ." Grace is not only where the Christian life begins. It is the soil in which we grow. We never graduate from grace. Every day we can learn to rest in it more, to receive it more deeply, and to extend it more freely. And we grow in the knowledge of Jesus, not just facts about Him, but deeper friendship with Him. Growth is often slow and quiet, like a tree adding rings year after year. You may not notice it from day to day. But looking back, you can see how far God has brought you. Peter ends with praise: "To him be glory both now and for ever." The goal of our growth is His glory. Today, take a small step toward deeper grace and knowledge of Jesus. Read a passage slowly. Pray honestly. Let grace keep doing its quiet work.
question: What small step could you take today to grow in grace and in the knowledge of Jesus?
prayer: Lord Jesus, I want to grow in grace and in the knowledge of You. Draw me deeper into friendship with You, and let my growth bring You glory. Amen.

text: Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.
reflection: In the Old Testament, priests offered animal sacrifices again and again, year after year. Those sacrifices pointed to something greater, but they could never fully remove sin. Then Jesus came: "Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us." Once, not repeatedly. By His own blood, not by another. And the result is eternal redemption, not temporary relief. What Jesus accomplished on the cross is complete and permanent. Nothing needs to be added to it. No repeated sacrifice is required. This means you can stop trying to pay for your own failures. You do not need to punish yourself or prove your worth over and over. Jesus has already obtained your redemption, and it is eternal. Today, rest in the finished work of Christ. Let His once-for-all sacrifice silence every accusing voice. Your redemption is secure.
question: What accusing voice needs to be silenced by Christ's once-for-all sacrifice?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You entered the holy place once by Your own blood and obtained eternal redemption for me. Let Your finished work silence every accusing voice in my heart. Amen.

text: Grace be to you and peace from God the Father, and from our Lord Jesus Christ…
reflection: Paul wrote to the Galatians with urgency. They were drifting from the gospel of grace, adding rules and requirements to what Christ had freely given. Yet even in a letter of correction, Paul began with a blessing: "Grace be to you and peace from God the Father, and from our Lord Jesus Christ." In the very next verse, he explains why grace is possible: Jesus "gave himself for our sins." Grace is not cheap. It cost the life of God's Son. That is why it is so precious, and why Paul was so concerned when people tried to replace it with performance. It is easy to drift into thinking that we must earn God's favor through effort. But grace and peace come from God, not from our achievements. Today, if you have been weighed down by the pressure to perform spiritually, come back to grace. Receive it as a gift, purchased by Jesus. And let His peace replace the anxiety of striving.
question: Where have you been weighed down by pressure to perform spiritually?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You gave Yourself for my sins, and Your grace is not cheap. Free me from the anxiety of striving, and let Your peace fill my heart. Amen.

text: But as for me, my prayer is unto thee, O LORD, in an acceptable time: O God, in the multitude of thy mercy hear me, in the truth of thy salvation.
reflection: The psalmist was in deep trouble, mocked and surrounded by those who hated him. Yet he turned to God with this prayer: "But as for me, my prayer is unto thee, O LORD, in an acceptable time: O God, in the multitude of thy mercy hear me." Notice the words but as for me. Others may mock, but he will pray. Others may turn away, but he will turn toward God. And he appeals not to his own goodness but to the multitude of God's mercy. God's mercy is not scarce. It is abundant, plentiful, more than we can count. When we come to Him in our distress, we come to an overflowing fountain. Today may be your acceptable time. Whatever is pressing on you, choose to pray rather than despair. Appeal to God's endless mercy. And as you receive it, let it overflow toward others who need mercy from you. The multitude of His mercy is enough for you and for them.
question: In your trouble today, how can you choose to pray rather than despair?
prayer: Lord, in the multitude of Your mercy, hear me. When trouble comes, help me turn to You in prayer, and let Your mercy overflow through me to others. Amen.

text: For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
reflection: Paul explains how faith takes hold of salvation: "For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." Faith begins deep inside, in the heart. It is not just agreeing with facts but trusting Jesus with your whole self. And then that inner faith naturally finds expression through the mouth. We confess, openly declaring that Jesus is Lord. Heart and mouth belong together. A faith that never speaks may be timid or uncertain. Words that are not backed by the heart are empty. But when what we believe inside is what we say outside, faith becomes whole. You do not have to be eloquent. A simple confession, Jesus is my Lord, is enough. Today, let what you believe in your heart find its way to your lips. Thank God out loud for saving you. Share your faith with someone. Speak the words that declare whom you trust. Faith grows stronger when it is spoken.
question: How can you let what you believe in your heart find its way to your lips today?
prayer: Lord Jesus, I believe in my heart that You are Lord. Give me courage to confess it with my mouth, to thank You out loud, and to share my faith with someone. Amen.

text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.
reflection: Paul closes his letter to the Corinthians with a blessing that has been spoken over churches for centuries: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." In one sentence, we meet the Father, Son, and Spirit, each offering a precious gift. From Jesus comes grace, His undeserved kindness. From the Father comes love, the source of everything good. From the Spirit comes communion, fellowship with God and with one another. And notice the final words: with you all. Not just the mature believers or the ones who agreed with Paul, but everyone, including those who had caused him pain. This blessing reminds us that God's love creates community. We are not meant to live our faith alone. The Spirit draws us together. Today, let this blessing shape your relationships. Extend grace, show love, and seek fellowship. Speak this blessing over your family, your church, or a friend who needs it.
question: Whom could you bless today with grace, love, and fellowship?
prayer: Lord Jesus, Father, and Holy Spirit, let Your grace, love, and communion be with me. Help me extend grace, show love, and seek fellowship with those around me. Amen.

text: And, behold, two blind men sitting by the way side, when they heard that Jesus passed by, cried out, saying, Have mercy on us, O Lord, thou Son of David.
reflection: Two blind men sat by the roadside near Jericho, unable to see the crowd passing by. But they could hear. And when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, "Have mercy on us, O Lord, thou Son of David." The crowd told them to be quiet. They only cried louder. And Jesus stopped. He asked what they wanted, touched their eyes, and restored their sight. Then they followed Him. These men could not see the road ahead, but they knew who could help them. Their guidance began with a cry for mercy. Sometimes we cannot see our way forward. We feel stuck by the roadside while life rushes past. But Jesus still passes by, and He still stops for those who call on Him. Do not let other voices silence your prayer. Cry out for mercy. He hears. And once He opens your eyes, follow Him. The path ahead becomes clear when you walk behind Jesus.
question: What do you need to cry out to Jesus for, even if other voices tell you to be quiet?
prayer: Lord Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me. Open my eyes to see what I cannot see on my own, and help me follow You on the road ahead. Amen.

text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.
reflection: Paul ends his first letter to the Thessalonians with one simple sentence: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you." After all the teaching, encouragement, and instruction, his final word is grace. That is fitting, because grace is both where the Christian life begins and where it continues. Paul had just given many commands: rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything. Those are high callings. But he does not leave his readers to accomplish them in their own strength. He wraps everything in grace. Whatever God asks of you, His grace goes with you to make it possible. You are never left to obey alone. As you begin this week, let grace have the last word over every responsibility and challenge. When the to-do list feels long, when relationships feel hard, when you feel you are falling short, remember that grace is with you. It is enough for today, and it will be enough for tomorrow.
question: Where are you feeling that you fall short today, and how can you remember that grace is with you?
prayer: Lord Jesus, Your grace is with me. When the list feels long and I fall short, remind me that Your grace is enough for today and tomorrow. Amen.

text: For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.
reflection: John draws a contrast between two great gifts: "For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ." The law was good. It revealed God's holiness and showed people how to live. But it could not change hearts or remove guilt. Then Jesus came, full of grace and truth. Notice that both arrive together. Grace without truth would be sentimental, pretending that sin does not matter. Truth without grace would be crushing, exposing sin with no remedy. But in Jesus, we find both perfectly joined. He tells us the truth about ourselves, and He meets that truth with overwhelming grace. This is why people of every background were drawn to Him. Sinners found welcome, and the proud found honest correction. Today, receive both from Jesus. Let Him speak truth into the areas of your life that need change. And let His grace hold you as He does it. In Him, you are fully known and fully loved.
question: What truth does Jesus want to speak into your life, and how can His grace hold you as He does?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You came full of grace and truth. Speak truth into the places in me that need change, and hold me with Your grace as You do. Amen.

text: But the God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you.
reflection: Peter knew suffering, and he wrote to people who were suffering. But he did not leave them in despair. He gave them a promise: "the God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you." Notice the phrase a while. Suffering is real, but it is not forever. And notice the four promises. God will make you perfect, restoring what is broken. He will stablish you, making you firm. He will strengthen you, giving you power to endure. And He will settle you, placing you on a solid foundation. These are not things we do for ourselves. They are things the God of all grace does in us. He uses even our hardest seasons to build something strong and lasting. If you are in a season of pain, hold on. The God of all grace has not forgotten you. He is restoring, strengthening, and settling you.
question: What in your life needs God's restoring, strengthening, and settling after a season of suffering?
prayer: God of all grace, my suffering is only for a while. Restore what is broken in me, make me steady, give me strength, and settle my heart on You. Amen.

text: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people…
reflection: Zechariah had been silent for months, unable to speak because he doubted the angel's message. But when his son John was born, his tongue was loosed, and his first words were praise: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people." After centuries of waiting, God had come near. He had visited His people. And He had begun the work of redemption that would be completed in Jesus. Zechariah's song reminds us that God does not save from a distance. He comes close. He enters our world, our history, and our personal stories. He visits us in our need and redeems what was lost. Perhaps you have been waiting a long time for God to act. Perhaps doubt has kept you quiet. Zechariah's story shows that God keeps His promises, even when we struggle to believe. Today, look for the ways God has visited you. Then join Zechariah in praise. Blessed be the Lord, who comes near to redeem.
question: Where has God visited you recently, and how can you praise Him for it?
prayer: Blessed be the Lord, who has visited and redeemed His people. Open my eyes to the ways You have come near to me, and fill my mouth with praise. Amen.

text: And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.
reflection: A jailer in Philippi was about to take his own life. An earthquake had opened the prison doors, and he assumed the prisoners had escaped. But Paul called out, telling him they were all still there. Trembling, the jailer asked what he must do to be saved. The answer was beautifully simple: "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house." That very night, he and his whole household believed and were baptized. This verse shows us how simple and how powerful the gospel is. Salvation is not a complicated program or a long list of requirements. It comes through trusting Jesus. And its impact spreads to families and households. As this month of grace and redemption ends, consider the people in your home and circle. Pray for them by name. Ask God to bring salvation to your household. And rest in the beautiful simplicity of the gospel: believe on the Lord Jesus Christ.
question: Who in your home or circle can you pray for by name, asking God to bring them to faith?
prayer: Lord Jesus, I believe on You, and I thank You for saving me. I pray for those in my household by name: bring them to You and save them. Amen.
